newsitem.title: ITALY: Di Pietro proved unconvential, colourful minister.
newsitem.headline: Di Pietro proved unconvential, colourful minister.

text.p: Former magistrate Antonio Di Pietro, the popular hero whose corruption investigations helped topple a governing class, lit up the chaotic world of Italian politics during his explosive six-month spell in the cabinet.

His earthiness, colourful language and utter lack of diplomacy shook parliament and many politicians will have breathed a sigh of relief at his announcement on Thursday that he would quit as public works minister.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi asked him to reconsider, an appeal that appeared to have fallen on deaf ears.
But, even if the charismatic, temperamental southerner does leave the cabinet, he may not stay out of politics for long.

Ever in the public eye, Di Pietro, 46, walked out of Prodi's centre-left administration after himself coming under investigation over alleged malpractice during his time in the elite team of Milan anti-graft magistrates.
Di Pietro, who is now making a habit of dramatic resignations, stormed out of the "Clean Hands" pool of prosecutors under mysterious circumstances in December 1994.
With a huge public following, all political parties sought to sign him up to their cause.
A coy Di Pietro, seen by some commentators as a man of the right, at first shunned the advances but in May he surprised many by agreeing to join Prodi's newly elected government.
Sauntering into parliament in jeans and boating shoes, his unconventional approach to power raised eyebrows.

But if he appeared laid back in public, at the ministry he set about work with a burst of activity, unleashing a tidal wave of projects aimed at getting Italy's public infrastructure programme, stalled by his own graft probes, back on its feet.
His plans soon brought him into conflict with coalition party the Greens, who threatened to quit the government if Di Pietro charged ahead with a motorway extension scheme.

"His idea of public works is 19th century," the Greens' leader, Carlo Ripa di Meana complained. "His imagination is filled with viaducts and tunnels - everything that recent thinking has put under suspicion."
But Di Pietro was backed by Prodi and the plans went ahead.
Anyone who saw Di Pietro operate in Milan's courthouse will not have been surprised at his workrate in the ministry.

It was Di Pietro, policeman turned public prosecutor, who ordered the fateful arrest in February 1992 of a corrupt local Socialist Party official, the prologue to a scandal which changed the face of Italian politics.
Di Pietro pursued the investigations with total commitment and his popularity and fame grew as the probes enveloped the upper echelons of public life.

The list of Di Pietro's "victims" reads like a Who's Who of the old political class, including former prime ministers Bettino Craxi and Arnaldo Forlani, and also one of the chief representives of the new political era, Silvio Berlusconi.

But the man who was dubbed "Mr Clean" sensationally quit the magistrature amid rumours that he had been forced out. He emerged with his reputation intact earlier this year from allegations of abuse of office that were thrown out of court.

Berlusconi's brother and business partner Paolo, as well as Cesare Previti, who was defence minister in Berlusconi's government in 1994, are both currently on trial accused of extortion against Di Pietro. They deny the charges.

Recent opinion polls show undented huge support for the superstar of the judicial assault on graft, making his blessing for any political party, or one of his own, a sure fire hit at any future election.
